examples.problem_statement: Examine the case of $\frac{1}{29}$: Begin with 1 (as usual) at the extreme right end and go on multiplying by 3 each time, “carrying over” the surplus digit or digits (if any) to the left (i.e. to be added to the next product to be determined). Thus, when we have obtained 14 digits i.e. ………………9 6 5 5 1 7 2 4 1 3 7 9 3 1, we find that we have reached 28; we know we have done half the work; and we get the first 14 digits by simply subtracting each of the above digits from NINE. ·0 3 4 4 8 2 7 5 8 6 2 0 6 8/

solution.description: Write a single 1 at the far right of the workspace. Every digit of the decimal for 1/29 is generated leftward from this one seed, so nothing else is needed to begin.
Multiply the seed 1 by 3, the Ekadhika multiplier for 29 because 3 is one more than the 2 standing before the 9. The product 3 is a single digit, so write 3 to the left of the 1 and carry nothing.
Multiply the digit just written, 3, by 3 again. The product 9 still fits in one place, so write 9 as the next digit leftward and again there is nothing to carry.
Multiply 9 by 3 to get 27. Only one digit may occupy each place, so write the units digit 7 and hold the tens digit 2 as a carry to be added into the next product.
Multiply the newly written 7 by 3 and add the carry of 2, giving 23. Write the units digit 3 and carry the 2 forward, repeating exactly the pattern set in the previous step.

Keep repeating this multiply-and-carry cycle until fourteen digits stand in the row. Read from the left they are 9, 6, 5, 5, 1, 7, 2, 4, 1, 3, 7, 9, 3, 1, and reaching 28 signals that half the 28-digit period is done.

Because the period is 28 digits long and the fourteen already found are its second half, the first half need not be multiplied out at all. Each of its digits is simply nine minus the corresponding digit of the half in hand.
Carry out that subtraction on 9, 6, 5, 5, 1, 7, 2, 4, 1, 3, 7, 9, 3, 1 in order, which produces 0, 3, 4, 4, 8, 2, 7, 5, 8, 6, 2, 0, 6, 8 as the first fourteen digits.
Place the complemented first half in front of the multiplied second half to read off the complete 28-digit recurring period of 1/29.

examples.problem_statement: Take $\frac{1}{39}$. Take 1 again at the extreme right end and continually multiply by 4 from the right to the left. Thus, we have: $\frac{1}{39}=\cdot025641.$

solution.operation: Start with 1 at the extreme right end.
solution.description: Seed the workspace with a single 1 at the far right, exactly as in the 1/29 case; only the multiplier will differ.

solution.operation: Multiply by 4 repeatedly from right to left.
solution.description: Because 39 ends in 9 with a 3 before it, the Ekadhika multiplier here is 4. Multiply repeatedly by 4, moving leftward and carrying any surplus digit into the following product.
The multiplications close on themselves after only six digits, giving 025641 as the entire recurring block for 1/39 rather than the long period seen with 29.

solution.operation: Note that complements from 9 do not apply here, only from 6.
solution.description: Do not reach for the complement-from-nine shortcut here. Since 39 is not prime but 3 times 13, the two halves of 025641 pair to 6 rather than to 9, so the nine-complement rule used for 1/29 simply does not apply.

{'point': 'that the two halves are not complementary with regard to 9 but only in relation to 6!'}

Writing the whole product into one place, for example putting 27 down instead of writing 7 and carrying the 2 into the next multiplication.
Applying the complement-from-nine rule to 1/39, whose halves are complements with respect to 6, not 9.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal representation of $\frac{1}{49}$ using Vedic methods.

solution.description: Rewrite 1/49 as 1/7 divided by 7. Since 1/7 is the familiar 0.142857 repeating, the task becomes dividing a known decimal by 7 instead of attacking 49 head on.

solution.operation: Avoid direct long division (which would require 42 steps)
solution.description: Set aside plain long division before starting. The period of 1/49 is 42 digits long, so the direct route costs 42 division steps and invites a slip in almost every one of them.

solution.operation: Apply Ekādhika method: multiply from right to left by 5 or divide from left to right by 5
solution.description: Use the Ekadhika instead. The digit before the 9 in 49 is 4, so the multiplier is 5, and the digits may be produced either by multiplying right to left by 5 or by dividing left to right by 5.

solution.operation: After computing 21 digits, observe the remainder 48 (D ↔ N)
solution.description: Pause after 21 digits and read the remainder. Its value of 48 marks the midpoint of the 42-digit period, the point at which the remaining digits are already determined.

solution.operation: Write the full 42-digit recurring decimal by combining the first 21 digits with their 9-complements
solution.description: Finish without further division by writing each of the first 21 digits' complement from nine as the corresponding digit of the second half, then joining the two halves into the full 42-digit recurring block.

solution.description: For 1/7, the Ekādhika number is the multiplier that will help generate the decimal expansion. Since the denominator is 7, we use the Ekādhika method for division by numbers ending with 9.

solution.operation: Set up the division using Ekādhika method
solution.description: The Ekādhika method for 1/7 involves recognizing that 7 × 142857 = 999999, which is one less than 1,000,000. This gives us a repeating decimal of 142857.

solution.result: \text{Start with 1 (numerator)} \\ 1 \times 3 = 3 \quad \text{(since Ekādhika for 7 is 3)} \\ 3 \times 3 = 9 \\ 9 \times 3 = 27 \quad \text{(write 7, carry over 2)} \\ 7 \times 3 + 2 = 23 \quad \text{(write 3, carry over 2)} \\ 3 \times 3 + 2 = 11 \quad \text{(write 1, carry over 1)} \\ 1 \times 3 + 1 = 4
solution.description: Using the Ekādhika multiplier of 3 (one more than the last digit of 7), we multiply and carry over to generate the decimal digits.
The digits generated from the Ekādhika process are 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7, which repeat every 6 digits.
Multiplying the decimal by 7 should give us 1, confirming the correctness of the decimal expansion.

concept.technique_name: Ekanyunena Purvena (by one less than the previous one)
concept.sub_category: Ekadhikena Purvena (One More than the Previous)

examples.problem_statement: (1) In the case of 7 (as denominator), 143 × 999 = 142/857; and lo! these are the six recurring decimal digits in the answer!

solution.description: State plainly what is to be checked: whether the product 143 times 999 really comes out as 142857, the six repeating digits of one seventh.
Recall why 142857 is the target figure. Seven times 142857 is 999999, so one seventh equals 142857/999999, which is exactly why the sutra's product should reproduce those digits.

Apply the one-less-than shortcut rather than multiplying digit by digit. Because 999 is one short of 1000, the product 143 times 999 becomes 143 shifted three places minus 143 itself, that is 143000 minus 143.
Carry out that single subtraction. 143000 minus 143 is 142857, so the whole multiplication collapses into one easy take-away.
Confirm the meaning of the product by dividing it by 999999, which returns 0.142857142857..., the decimal for one seventh, so the six digits found are indeed the recurring block.

Compare the computed block against the figure quoted alongside the problem. The quoted 13076923 belongs to the thirteenths, not the sevenths, and does not match 142857, so the value derived here is the one to keep.

examples.problem_statement: (2) In the case of 13, 077 × 999 = 076/923; and these are the six digits in the recurring decimal equivalent of ¹⁄₁₃!

solution.operation: Multiply 077 by 999 using the Ekanyūna method.
solution.description: Run the same one-less-than shortcut on 077: multiplying by 999 means writing 77000 and subtracting 77, which gives 076923. Dividing that by 999999 shows these six digits are the recurring block of one thirteenth.

examples.problem_statement: (3) In the case of 17, 05882353 × 99999999 = 05882352/94117647; and these are the 16 recurring digits in the recurring decimal equivalent of ¹⁄₁₇!

solution.description: Scale the identical idea up to eight digits. Multiplying 05882353 by 99999999 means shifting it eight places and subtracting the original, giving 05882352 followed by 94117647, the sixteen recurring digits of one seventeenth.

examples.problem_statement: Analyze the successive remainders of the fraction 1/7.

solution.description: Set 1 divided by 7 up as an ordinary long division. The quotient digits are familiar, but it is the successive remainders that this problem is really after, so keep them visible at every stage.
Annex a zero to the 1 to make 10. Seven goes into 10 once, so the first quotient digit is 1 and the first remainder is 3.
Annex a zero to the remainder 3 to make 30. Seven goes into 30 four times, giving quotient digit 4 and remainder 2.
Annex a zero to the remainder 2 to make 20. Seven goes into 20 twice, giving quotient digit 2 and remainder 6.
Annex a zero to the remainder 6 to make 60. Seven goes into 60 eight times, giving quotient digit 8 and remainder 4.
Annex a zero to the remainder 4 to make 40. Seven goes into 40 five times, giving quotient digit 5 and remainder 5.
Annex a zero to the remainder 5 to make 50. Seven goes into 50 seven times, giving quotient digit 7 and remainder 1. That remainder of 1 is the starting value again, so the cycle has closed.
Collect the remainders in the order they appeared: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5. There are six of them, matching the six-digit period of the decimal.

Pair the first remainder with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on. Each pair adds to 7, so the second half of the remainder cycle is the complement of the first with respect to the divisor.

examples.answer: The remainders are: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5. They are complementary pairs that sum to 7: (1,6), (3,4), (2,5).

examples.problem_statement: Analyze the successive remainders of the fraction 1/13.

solution.description: Divide 1 by 13 the same way and record every remainder in the order it appears, continuing until the starting remainder 1 returns and so fixes the length of the cycle.
Split the recorded list into two equal halves and write the second half directly beneath the first so that corresponding remainders stand in the same column.
Add each column. Every pair totals 13, the divisor, which shows the second half of the remainder cycle is the complement of the first exactly as the sevenths were complementary to 7.

examples.answer: The remainders are complementary and sum to the divisor 13.

concept.technique_name: Ekadhikena Purvena (By one more than the previous one) and cyclic number patterns

examples.problem_statement: In the case of $\frac{1}{17}$, the successive remainders are: $10, 15, 14, 4, 6, 9, 5, 16, 7, 2, 3, 13, 11, 8, 12, 1$. The last 8 remainders are complements from 17 of the first eight ones. Similarly, for $\frac{1}{19}$, the remainders are: $10, 15, 12, 6, 3, 11, 15, 17, 18, 9, 4, 7, 13, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1$, where the first nine remainders, when added successively to the next nine, give 19 each time. Using this pattern, find the recurring decimal equivalent of $\frac{2}{7}$ given that $\frac{1}{7} = 0.\overline{142857}$.

solution.description: Take the decimal for one seventh as the given starting fact. Everything that follows rearranges or scales these six digits rather than dividing afresh.
Since two sevenths is twice one seventh, the answer can be obtained by doubling the known repeating decimal instead of running a new division.
Double the repeating block digit by digit, carrying where a product passes 9. The block 142857 becomes 285714 and the doubling repeats identically on every subsequent cycle.
The six digits 285714 recur without end, so the answer is written once with a bar over the block rather than as a trailing string of dots.

Cross-check against the remainder cycle. Dividing 1 by 7 gives remainders 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5; doubling each of those modulo 7 gives 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3, which is the remainder cycle for two sevenths and agrees with the digits just produced.
Note what the doubling actually did: 142857 times 2 is 285714, the very same six digits started at a different point. This cyclic property is why every seventh reuses one ring of digits.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 2/7.

solution.description: Rank the six digits of the ring 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7 in ascending order as 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, then take the entry whose rank equals the numerator 2. That entry is the digit 2.
Enter the ring at that digit 2 and read the six digits round clockwise without changing their order, which gives 285714 as the recurring block for 2/7.

concept.technique_name: cyclic rotation of the recurring block

examples.problem_statement: What is the decimal equivalent of fractions from 1/13 to 12/13?

solution.description: Establish the base cycle first. Dividing 1 by 13 the Vedic way returns a six-digit repeating block, 076923, and every other thirteenth will be read off from blocks like this one.
Double that block to reach two thirteenths. The result 153846 is a genuinely new ring, not a re-entry into 076923, so the thirteenths are not served by a single cycle the way the sevenths are.
Fix the two rings now that both are known. Every fraction from 1/13 to 12/13 is one of these two six-digit blocks entered at a different starting digit.

List the first six multiples and note which ring each belongs to: 1/13, 3/13 and 4/13 are entries into 076923, while 2/13, 5/13 and 6/13 are entries into 153846. The two families alternate rather than running in order.

List the remaining six the same way. 9/13, 10/13 and 12/13 are entries into the 076923 ring, and 7/13, 8/13 and 11/13 are entries into the 153846 ring, so all twelve are now accounted for by the two blocks.

Check the whole table by pairing fractions that sum to one. 1/13 plus 12/13 is 13/13, and their blocks 076923 and 923076 add digit for digit to 999999, confirming the rings were entered at the right points.

examples.problem_statement: Decimalise $\frac{3}{7}$

solution.operation: Recognize that $\frac{3}{7} = \frac{21}{49}$, so Ekādhika Pūrva is 5.
solution.description: Multiply numerator and denominator of 3/7 by 7 to reach 21/49. The denominator now ends in 9, and since the digit standing before that 9 is 4, the Ekadhika Purva multiplier is 5.

solution.operation: Divide by 5 in the usual manner to obtain the quotient digits 4, 2, 8.
solution.description: Divide the numerator 21 by 5 in the ordinary way, prefixing each remainder to the front of the next digit before dividing again. This yields the quotient digits 4, 2 and 8.

solution.operation: Observe that the dividend becomes 28, which is less than 49 (D < N).
solution.description: Watch the running dividend rather than counting steps. It has now reached 28, which is smaller than the denominator 49, and that is the signal that half the period is complete and the division can stop.

solution.operation: Write the last three quotient digits as complements from nine: 5, 7, 1.
solution.description: Fill in the remaining three digits without dividing, by taking complements from nine of the digits already found: 4 becomes 5, 2 becomes 7 and 8 becomes 1, completing the block 428571.

solution.operation: Alternatively, continue division until dividend becomes 21 (starting point), confirming recurrence.
solution.description: As an independent check, ignore the shortcut and keep dividing. When the dividend returns to the starting value 21 the period has closed, confirming that the same six digits recur.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note 1: For decimalising fractions like $\\frac{1}{7}, \\frac{2}{7}, \\dots$, simply divide multiples of 10 (10,20,30,...) by 7 and use the remainder as the starting point — work proceeds automatically.'}
{'point': 'This enables rapid mental computation without performing full division.'}
common_mistakes: Using 7 or 9 as the divisor for 21/49. The Ekadhika is 5, one more than the 4 that stands before the 9.
Taking complements from ten instead of nine, which turns 4, 2, 8 into 6, 8, 2 and wrecks the second half of the block.
Forgetting to prefix each remainder to the next digit while dividing by 5, which loses the carry that links one quotient digit to the next.
repair_note: Deleted one auto-extracted QC_TRAP filler object from common_mistakes and wrote three real hazards for the 21/49 work. Rewrote all five descriptions so each names its own quantities; the originals were generic instructions ('Apply complement from nine to get remaining decimal digits') that never mentioned the digits 4, 2, 8 or their complements 5, 7, 1. Changed scaffold from number_line to place_value_chart, since the steps build a row of quotient digits with remainders prefixed and use no linear scale.
